So, let me begin with a brief overview of Kanohar Electricals. Kanohar has been in the electrical 
equipment business for over 40 years, with our journey dating back to 1972. Over the years, we 
have steadily evolved from a small electrical equipment manufacturer into a specialized player. 
Today, we focus on high-value, technically demanding products for India’s transmission, 
railways, and renewable energy infrastructure. 
 
Our flagship business is Power Transformers. We manufacture Power Transformers up to 500 
MVA and 400 kV; Scott-connected Transformers up to 100 MVA and 220 and 132 kV for Indian

Railways; and shunt reactors up to 125 MVAR and 400 kV. As of FY26, our Transformer 
business contributes around 85% of our revenues. 
 
Alongside manufacturing, we have built an EPC business covering substations and transmission 
lines. It contributes roughly 15% of the revenues, but it is strategically important. Indian utilities 
sometimes bundle transformers into larger substation packages, and our EPC capability allows 
us to bid for those packages directly. This widens our total addressable market, or TAM, and 
improves our win rates. 
 
Our manufacturing operations are based at two facilities in Meerut: Rithani and Gangol, with a 
combined capacity of approximately 19,200 MVA. The Gangol facility, with a capacity of 
around 18,000 MVA, is our key facility for large power transformers and shunt reactors. 
 
Coming to the industry environment and opportunity, we believe India is entering a structurally 
strong investment cycle in power transmission and railways infrastructure. Power demand is 
rising rapidly. This is driven by multiple tailwinds like industrialization, urbanization, 
electrification, data centers, electric mobility, and a broader shift towards a more electricity-
intensive economy. 
 
At the same time, India is adding significant renewable generation capacity, but generation 
capacity can only become usable power when adequate transmission infrastructure is in place. 
And this makes the transmission grid a critical enabler of India’s energy transition. 
 
We are also seeing a broader focus on energy security and domestic power infrastructure. The 
growing importance of reliable and indigenous power infrastructure is likely to support 
investment across the transmission ecosystem over the medium to long term. 
 
An important new layer is intra-state transmission. Until now, much of the demand has come 
from inter-state projects. Now, state utilities, such as those in Maharashtra and Gujarat, are 
raising capital, announcing large programs of their own. 
 
At the state level, 400 kV is typically the highest voltage, and that plays to our strengths. In this 
context, as you are all aware, recently, Government of India announced the Green Energy 
Corridor III, which is entirely focused on the intra-state transmission with a ₹1.85 lakh crores 
outlay. 
 
The railway sector is another important opportunity for us. India is investing significantly in 
railway electrification, dedicated freight corridors, Vande Bharat, and high-speed rail. These 
projects require specialized transformers and related electrical infrastructure. 
 
India has already electrified about 99.6% of its broad-gauge network. Future electrification, 
whether new lines or replacements, will move to the 2x25 kV AC system needed for the high-
speed and heavy-haul traffic, including Vande Bharat services and dedicated freight corridors. 
So, that system needs the Scott-connected transformers, and that is exactly where we are present. 
 
Based on the industry and railway requirements, we see a significant opportunity for these 
specialized transformer products over the next several years. The common thread across both of

these markets is that participation is qualification-driven, and this is an important aspect of our 
industry and business. 
 
Factory capacity in our industry is not the same as being able to bid to be eligible for large utility 
and railway tenders. A manufacturer needs two things: first is the past performance experience, 
which means its transformers have run satisfactorily in the field for a defined period; and second, 
a short-circuit certification for that specific rating. 
 
Short-circuit certification is demanding. A prototype unit is designed, it is built, it is sent to a 
government lab such as CPRI or National High Power Test Laboratory, and there it must 
withstand the simulated fault conditions. For a large unit like a 500 MVA Transformer, the 
journey from concept to certificate in hand takes anywhere from 18 to 24 months. 
 
Kanohar has completed more than 200 successful short-circuit tests at a government laboratory, 
and today, we are one among the few manufacturers in India certified for the 500 MVA 400 kV 
Transformers. In railways, we were the first Indian company to receive the RDSO approval for 
a 100 MVA 220 kV Scott-connected transformer, and today, we are one of the two companies 
certified at that rating. Similarly, at the 100 MVA 132 kV rating, we are one among four. 
 
These qualifications matter because they make us eligible for larger and more technically 
demanding tenders. Apart from this, over the years, we have built a unique portfolio of 
qualifications, not just for transformer, but across transformers, power transformers, railways 
transformers, shunt reactors, and also EPC of substations and transmission lines. We believe this 
combination gives us a differentiated position. 
 
In terms of the product mix and backward integration, between FY24 and FY26, our product 
mix has evolved significantly towards the premium products. The contribution of 400 kV 
Transformers increased from 10.3% in FY24 to 52% in FY26 and stood at about 70% in Q1 of 
FY27. 
 
Our qualifications made us eligible for the large orders, and this is reflected in the portfolio mix 
that is moving towards the more premium, high-value business. We have also invested in 
backward integration for several critical components, including transformer tanks, control 
panels, radiators, and insulation components. 
 
Individually, these components may not be a large part of the overall transformer value, but 
making them in-house gives us greater control over quality, reliability, and delivery timelines. 
In terms of our strategy and the road ahead, our strategy is simple: we'll keep expanding into the 
premium, qualification-driven products in the transmission and railways and add capacity ahead 
of demand while staying financially disciplined. 
 
On the capacity side, we are planning a brownfield expansion of about 18,000 MVA at our 
Gangol plant. Part of the proceeds from the IPO will be used for this expansion. Based on our 
current trajectory, our existing capacity is sufficient through FY28, and we aim to have this new 
capacity in place for FY29, well before we approach our limits.

On 765 kV, this is our next major step. We already have the technology in place. Interestingly,

On the railways side, as the sector enters a major upgrade cycle, we expect strong demand for 
Scott-connected transformers, and we are simultaneously also adding other specialized railway 
transformers to our portfolio. 
 
Coming to our order book, as of 30th June, our order book stand at 2,026 crores. Industry lead 
times are currently around 18 to 24 months, so the tenders we are bidding for today are largely 
for the execution in FY29 and beyond. 
 
On working capital, our business carries roughly 120 days of receivables and 80 days of 
inventory, offset by 70 to 80 days of payables. This gives us a net working capital cycle of 
around 120 days. This reflects the size and long build cycle of large transformers, not the credit 
risk. Our customers are central and state transmission utilities and well-funded projects, and we 
have not faced any delinquencies of any kind. 
 
To sum up, Kanohar is a 54-year-old engineering company that has spent decades earning the 
right to compete at the top end of India's transformer market. We hold certifications that very 
few companies have, our order book gives us visibility, and the demand drivers in both power 
and railways are long-term. 
 
For FY27, H2 or the second half is expected to remain the key execution period, and we 
anticipate this trend to continue through the year. We are targeting a revenue of approximately 
INR950 crores with a broadly similar EBITDA margin profile as FY26. Growth will be driven 
by a healthy increase in manufacturing volumes and continued improvement in product mix, 
supported by a higher contribution from the 400 kV segment.
